Generating responses with mgcv family objects

Source: R/data-sim-families.R
data_sim_families.Rd

data_sim() accepts instantiated standard and mgcv family objects. The example template supplies covariates and true functions; predictors supplies the linear predictors; parameters supplies generating values that are not themselves modelled by a predictor. The "truth" attribute records all predictors, distribution parameters and complete responses.

Scalar families

The parameter names below belong inside parameters = list(...). Parameters are scalar unless explicitly described as observation-level. Beta draws use the constructor's eps endpoint adjustment, matching mgcv's generator. This adjustment can matter when the beta law places substantial probability very close to zero or one; eps is recorded in the truth.

FamilyGenerating parameters
gaussian()dispersion = 1, the non-negative variance
poisson(), cpois()None
binomial()trials = 1, positive integer trial counts
Gamma(), inverse.gaussian()dispersion = 1
nb(), negbin()theta, positive size; Inf gives the Poisson limit
tw(), Tweedie()power in (1, 2), and dispersion = 1
betar()Positive precision
scat()df above the family's min.df, and positive t scale sigma
ocat()Finite increasing cuts, one fewer than the categories
ziP()intercept and natural-scale slope above the constructor's b
cnorm(), clog()Positive sigma, Gaussian SD or logistic scale
bcg()lambda = 0 and positive log-response SD sigma

Dispersion and trials can have length one or n. All other scalar-family parameters are constant across observations. Fixed constructor parameters are used when available; conflicting explicit parameters are errors. Otherwise the corresponding generating values are required, including cut points for ocat(R = ...). For example, both family = mgcv::nb(theta = 3) and family = mgcv::nb(), parameters = list(theta = 3) specify size 3. Constructor starting values for an estimated parameter are not used as generating truth. A size range in negbin(c(1, 10)) also requires an explicit generating theta.

For ziP(), lambda = exp(eta) and P(Y > 0) = 1 - exp(-exp(intercept + slope * eta)). Positive observations follow a Poisson distribution conditioned on being positive. The natural slope includes the constructor's lower bound b; the second entry of ziP(theta = ...) is instead a log excess above b. For fixed ordinal spacings, mgcv fixes the first cut at -1; for example ocat(theta = c(1, 5)) supplies cuts c(-1, 0, 5). For free cuts whose first value is a, mgcv's fixed first cut of -1 represents the same probabilities after shifting the predictor by -(a + 1). Include the corresponding component intercept in grouped fitting recipes.

Quasi families do not define a complete sampling distribution and are rejected. Nonzero Box-Cox powers are currently rejected: some Gaussian transformed responses would lie outside the inverse transformation's domain.

Families with several linear predictors

The columns returned by predictors follow mgcv's order and links, including their constructor-specific bounds. These are link-scale predictors, not the mu arguments of mgcv's random-number generators.

FamilyPredictor order and natural parameters recorded in truth
gaulss()Mean, SD predictor; records mu, sigma
gammals()Log mean, log-dispersion predictor; records mu, dispersion
gumbls()Location, log-scale predictor; records location, mu (mean), sigma
gevlss()Location, log scale, shape predictor; records location, sigma, shape
shash()Location, scale predictor, skewness, log tail; records location, sigma, skewness, tail
twlss()Mean predictor, power predictor, log dispersion; records mu, power, dispersion
ziplss()Log Poisson intensity, complementary log-log presence predictor; records lambda, presence
multinom(K)K logits relative to category 0; records category probabilities
mvn(d)d response means; parameters$covariance defaults to the identity matrix

These families need no scalar generating parameters except mvn()'s optional positive definite covariance matrix. In shash(), the transformed normal is multiplied by tail * sigma, following mgcv's parameterisation. In gumbls(), the mean is location plus Euler's constant times sigma; the first predictor specifies the location. For gevlss(), the default shape link restricts shape to (-1, 0.5); the identity link allows any finite shape. In ziplss(), positive counts follow a zero-truncated Poisson distribution.

Default predictors

Let g be the template's f before distribution transformations. Scalar Gaussian, t, Gaussian-censoring, logistic-censoring and Box-Cox families use natural location g. Binomial and beta means are plogis((g - 5) / 5); ordinal location is g - mean(g); the ziP() predictor is g / 5. Other scalar means are exp(g / 5). Each mean is transformed with the supplied family's link. If it is outside that link's domain, supply custom predictors rather than relying on a default.

For general families, default predictors are: (g, 0) for gaulss() and gumbls(); (g / 5, 0) for gammals() and ziplss(); (g, 0, linkfun(0)) for gevlss() (zero shape under the supplied shape link); (g, 0, 0, 0) for shash(); and (g / 5, 0, 0) for twlss(). Multivariate normal means repeat g. Multinomial logit j is (g - mean(g)) / 5 * j / K. The sc_location_scale template instead supplies its own log mean and log dispersion for gammals().

Censoring and survival

For cnorm(), clog(), cpois() and bcg(), observation can contain finite left and right detection limits and a positive interval_width. Responses outside detection limits are left or right censored. Other responses are placed in rounding intervals wholly inside those limits; values in intervals crossing a limit are retained exactly. Omitting observation returns complete responses.

Matrix responses use equal entries for exact observations, (limit, -Inf) for left censoring, (limit, Inf) for right censoring, and (lower, upper) for intervals. bcg() instead uses zero in the second entry for left censoring; its limits must be positive. Poisson detection limits must be non-integer, and interval widths must be integer numbers of counts. Its intervals use half-integer endpoints to avoid ambiguity at count values.

cox.ph() uses Weibull cumulative baseline hazard H0(t) = (t / baseline_scale)^baseline_shape, with both baseline parameters defaulting to 1. Event times have survival exp(-H0(t) * exp(eta)). Independent exponential censoring has censor_rate = 0.2; zero disables censoring. Default eta is (g - mean(g)) / 5. Fit using weights = status. True event and censoring times are retained in the truth parameter list.

Grouped families

Supply family = mgcv::gfam(list(...)), optionally with parameters = list(components = list(...), index = ...). components contains one parameter list per family-list position. index is one integer position per row (a scalar selects the same family for every row). Without index, every component is represented at least once and remaining positions are sampled uniformly; n must be at least the number of families. Repeated family types retain separate indices and parameters.

The default shared predictor is g / 5; custom predictors return one column. Scalar response families are supported; general families are rejected. Censored-family components return complete, uncensored responses. Fit using cbind(y, index) as the response and weights = trials if a component is binomial with more than one trial. Row-level dispersion and trial vectors in component parameter lists align with the full generated data, or can have the component's row count. Truth parameters record each component's rows.

See also

data_sim(), data_sim_shapes, mgcv::family.mgcv()

Examples

# A beta response: precision is explicitly chosen, rather than estimated.
d <- data_sim(family = mgcv::betar(theta = 12), seed = 2)
attr(d, "truth")$parameters$precision
#> [1] 12

# Binomial proportions: use trials as the fitting weights.
d <- data_sim(family = binomial(), parameters = list(trials = 10), seed = 2)

# Mean and standard deviation have separate predictors.
d <- data_sim("gwf2", family = mgcv::gaulss(), seed = 2,
  predictors = function(d) cbind(d$f, log(0.2 + d$x)))

# Fit a censored normal model to the matrix response.
d <- data_sim("sc_increasing", family = mgcv::cnorm(theta = 0.2), seed = 2,
  observation = list(left = 0.1, right = 0.9))
# \donttest{
m <- mgcv::gam(y ~ s(x), family = mgcv::cnorm(), data = d, method = "REML")
# }
